draft.title: Spelling strategies for new words
card: Syllables
A syllable is one beat of sound in a word. Say the word slowly and clap each beat, then spell one beat at a time: won-der-ful has three.
Word parts
Many words are built from a base word plus a prefix at the start or a suffix at the end. Spot the parts and spell each one: un + happy + ness.
Spelling rules
Rules you already know can guide you. For example, a word that ends in a consonant plus y usually changes the y to i before an ending: happy becomes happiness.
Use these strategies together on an unfamiliar word. Split it, spell each part, then check the whole word.
draft.remember: Split a new word into beats and parts, then apply rules you know.

a.q: A student wants to spell the new word "adventurous". Which approach uses a spelling strategy from the card?
opts: Split it into syllables and spell each one in turn
Write it once and hope that it looks right
Spell it the way the first letter sounds
Copy the spelling of a word that rhymes with it
a.why: Splitting a long word into syllables lets the student spell it one small beat at a time. Guessing by how it looks is tempting, but it is not a strategy the card teaches, and rhyming words are often spelled differently.
a.clue: Which option breaks the word into smaller pieces?

b.q: Tane must spell "carefulness". He sees it is made of care + ful + ness. Which strategy is he using?
opts: Breaking the word into its base word and suffixes
Clapping the syllables of the word out loud
Changing a final y to i before an ending
Matching it to a word with a similar sound
b.why: Tane has split the word into a base word, care, and two suffixes, ful and ness. Clapping syllables is a different strategy, because it splits the word by sound beats and not by meaning parts. The word has no y to change.
b.clue: He split the word by its meaning parts, not its sound beats.

a.best: Split it into syllables and spell each one in turn

b.best: Breaking the word into its base word and suffixes

problems.detail: The word parts example 'un + happy + ness' tells students to spell each part. Spelling each part as written gives 'unhappyness', and the card never names the whole word 'unhappiness'. The y-to-i rule comes only in the next bullet, so the example could teach a wrong spelling unless it shows the joined word (un + happy + ness = unhappiness).

check.summary: Both questions are sound and have one clear answer each. The only issue is the word parts example 'un + happy + ness', which could lead students to write 'unhappyness'. It should show the joined spelling, unhappiness.
